Pivot or Persevere: Making Strategic Decisions
As your team moves through the cycle of building, measuring, and learning, you’ll eventually hit a crossroads. Do you keep going down the same path, or is it time to make a real change in direction?
This moment—the choice to pivot or persevere—is one of the biggest decisions you'll face in any startup or innovation journey.
Now, what exactly is a pivot? Think of it as a structured course correction. It’s not about throwing in the towel or admitting defeat. Instead, it’s about testing a new, fundamental hypothesis—whether that's about your product, your strategy, or even your whole business model.
Here’s something important: a pivot isn’t a sign you’ve failed. It’s a smart response when the evidence shows your current approach just isn’t leading to the sustainable growth you’re after.
There are actually quite a few ways to pivot, depending on what you’re learning from your experiments and your customers. Let me share a few of the most common types:
There’s the zoom-in pivot, where you realize one feature stands out as the most valuable. So, you turn that feature into the whole product.
Or maybe it’s a zoom-out pivot. If your original offering feels too narrow, you expand your product to include more features or services, aiming to better meet your customers’ needs.
Sometimes, a customer segment pivot is what’s needed. That’s when you shift your focus to a different group of customers—ones who show more interest or a stronger need for what you’re building.
There’s also the channel pivot, where you try a new way to deliver or sell your product, hoping to reach customers more effectively.
And don’t forget the technology pivot—that’s when you find a better technology to deliver the same solution, making things more efficient or scalable.
So, how do you know when to pivot or when to stick with your current plan? The answer lies in the data. It’s easy to trust your gut, but this decision deserves more.
By looking at the results of your experiments and tracking your key metrics, you’ll get a clear picture. If those metrics are moving in the right direction and customers are genuinely responding, keep refining and improving. But if progress stalls, or customers aren’t connecting, that’s your cue—it might be time for a pivot.
Of course, making the call to pivot isn’t always easy. There’s often a real emotional attachment to the original idea, and it can feel tough to admit when something’s not working. But here’s the truth: being willing to change course when the evidence calls for it? That’s what separates successful innovators from the rest.
One strategy that really helps is to schedule regular “pivot or persevere” meetings. In these sessions, the team comes together to review progress and openly discuss whether it’s time for a change. It creates a structured, honest space for reflection, and it keeps everyone from drifting off course without realizing it.
Remember, perseverance isn’t about stubbornly sticking with a plan when all signs point in another direction. It’s about keeping up the experiments and improvements, as long as there’s real progress. Pivoting, on the other hand, is about having the courage to try a new approach—one that might finally unlock your true potential.
Both paths—pivoting and persevering—take courage, discipline, and a real commitment to learning. But when you embrace the possibility of change, you avoid falling into the trap of sunk costs. And you give yourself the best shot at building something truly valuable.
